clue.text: Some fundamental changes made in Rome

definitions.text: Some fundamental changes made in Rome

parts.words: Some fundamental changes made in Rome
parts.note: reads as political upheaval in the Roman state, but points to Ovid's long poem of shape-shifting, written in Rome

explanation.surface: A remark about sweeping reforms carried out in the Roman capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Ovid's epic is a catalogue of transformations, people turned into trees, birds and stars, and he wrote it in Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: Ovid's poem takes its Greek title from transformations of form, which are changes at the most basic level.

clue.text: Strange appearance of Valery Richmond in Brackenbridge

indicators.note: a strange appearance means the letters of the name that follows show up in an unfamiliar arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone named Valery Richmond turns up oddly in a place called Brackenbridge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange appearance of' rearranges VALERY RICHMOND. The novel is by Hugh Henry Brackenridge (the clue prints an extra B), so 'in Brackenbridge' means a work found in that author's output.
explanation.definitionFit: The picaresque satire of early American politics is the best-known book written by Brackenridge.

clue.text: A super job for W. H. Davies?

definitions.text: A super job for W. H. Davies?

parts.words: A super job for W. H. Davies?
parts.note: reads as praise for some excellent post, but recalls the Welsh poet's book The Autobiography of a Super-...

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a poet landed a splendid post.
explanation.walkthrough: W. H. Davies spent years roaming America and Britain as a vagrant and wrote The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp; wandering of that kind was his 'job'.
explanation.definitionFit: A vagrant who wanders from place to place is the kind of life Davies described in his autobiography.

clue.text: A misunderstanding with the French

parts.note: reads as a diplomatic quarrel with France, but asks for the French word for a misunderstanding, also the title of a Camus play

explanation.surface: A diplomatic falling-out with France.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is French for 'badly heard', the everyday French word for a misunderstanding; Camus used it as the title of his 1944 play.
explanation.definitionFit: French speakers call a mix-up in which one party wrongly understood the other by this word.

clue.text: Arbiter may prepare savoury

indicators.note: preparing a dish means working its ingredients into shape, so the letters of the word arbiter are reworked

explanation.surface: A referee might cook up a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: Welsh rarebit is cheese on toast, a traditional British savoury course.
explanation.definitionFit: Melted cheese on toast is served as a savoury, the salty dish that ends a British dinner.

clue.text: Byron's Gladiator was not thus attentive to "the inhuman shout"

definitions.text: Byron's Gladiator was not thus attentive to "the inhuman shout"

parts.words: Byron's Gladiator was not thus attentive to "the inhuman shout"
parts.note: recalls the dying gladiator in Childe Harold, who 'heard it, but he heeded not' the inhuman shout of the arena crowd

explanation.surface: Byron's dying gladiator ignores the crowd's cruel roar.
explanation.walkthrough: In Childe Harold's Pilgrimage, Canto IV, the dying gladiator hears the inhuman shout hailing the victor but heeds it not; his thoughts are with his family far away.
explanation.definitionFit: Paying careful notice to something is to be attentive, a word the poem's 'heeded not' denies.

clue.text: It sets learning in use, pace Falstaff

definitions.text: It sets learning in use, pace Falstaff

parts.words: It sets learning in use, pace Falstaff
parts.note: echoes Falstaff's praise of sherris in Henry IV Part 2: learning is a mere hoard of gold till this wine sets it in act and use

explanation.surface: Falstaff's claim about what puts knowledge to work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pace' means 'according to' here. Falstaff's sherris-sack was a fortified white wine from Spain, which he said brings a man's learning into action.
explanation.definitionFit: The old name for the dry Spanish wine that Falstaff drank and praised so loudly.

clue.text: Figaro's tradecraft could have made it Barbiere the first

definitions.text: Figaro's tradecraft could have made it Barbiere the first

parts.words: Figaro's tradecraft could have made it Barbiere the first
parts.note: Figaro is the Barber of Seville, so the lather of his trade could turn Il Barbiere, an opera, into the first of a lighter genre

explanation.surface: The barber's skills might have made Rossini's opera a pioneer.
explanation.walkthrough: A barber works with lather, so Rossini's Il Barbiere di Siviglia, an opera about a barber, would be the first opera of that kind: a pun on the term for a broadcast serial drama.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-running broadcast serial drama about everyday lives, named for the detergent firms that first sponsored them.

clue.text: Record created by Beckett

parts.note: reads as a recording the playwright made, but points to his one-act play in which an old man plays back the reel he recorded years before

explanation.surface: A recording made by the playwright Samuel Beckett.
explanation.walkthrough: Beckett's 1958 play has its single character listen to a tape recording he made thirty years earlier, so the play itself is a 'record'.
explanation.definitionFit: Beckett's one-act play centres on an old man's reel-to-reel recording, his final one, made on his birthday.

clue.text: Somehow belied air of mischief

indicators.note: somehow means in some unexplained way, so the letters of belied air come out in a different order

explanation.surface: A mischievous manner that somehow contradicted itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Devilish behaviour, from the French for devil, is wicked mischief or sorcery.

clue.text: Many a musical seat

parts.note: reads as a seat at a concert, but points to the party game in which several seats are fought over when the music stops

explanation.surface: A remark about seats at a concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: In the party game musical chairs there are many such seats, one fewer than players each round.
explanation.definitionFit: A seat with a back, many of which feature in the children's game played to music.

clue.text: Mature start for Waugh novel

annotationWithheld.why: Mature start for Waugh novel (5): 'Mature' defines the answer, but no Waugh novel or other reading of 'start for Waugh novel' gives these letters

clue.text: The Emperor was in it

parts.note: reads as an emperor inside some place, but recalls Andersen's tale of the Emperor's new clothes, in which he parades naked

explanation.surface: A statement that an emperor was present somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In the buff' means naked; Andersen's Emperor walked out in his invisible new clothes, wearing nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom 'in the buff' means wearing nothing, which is how the Emperor paraded in Andersen's tale.

clue.text: "Take physic, —;/ Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel" (King Lear)

definitions.text: "Take physic, —;/ Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel" (King Lear)

parts.words: "Take physic, —;/ Expose thyself to feel what wretches feel" (King Lear)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Lear on the heath addresses grandeur itself, telling it to take its medicine

explanation.surface: Lear's speech in the storm urging the great to feel the suffering of the poor.
explanation.walkthrough: In Act 3 Scene 4 Lear, out in the storm, tells splendour and greatness to take its medicine and feel what the poor feel.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceremonial splendour and grandeur, which Lear addresses as if it were a person.

clue.text: Carelessly relate bare name of rumourmonger

indicators.note: doing something carelessly leaves it in disorder, so the letters of relate bare are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone casually passes on a bare name, the way gossips do.
explanation.definitionFit: A gossip who spreads stories and secrets is the same as a rumourmonger.

clue.text: His poems were Certain and Elegant, his ballad Proper and New

definitions.text: His poems were Certain and Elegant, his ballad Proper and New

parts.words: His poems were Certain and Elegant, his ballad Proper and New
parts.note: reads as praise, but quotes titles: Certain Elegant Poems (1647) and A Proper New Ballad, called The Fairies' Farewell

explanation.surface: An admirer praising a poet's verses and ballad.
explanation.walkthrough: Richard Corbet(t), Bishop of Oxford and Norwich, wrote A Proper New Ballad (The Fairies' Farewell); his verse was collected as Certain Elegant Poems.
explanation.definitionFit: The seventeenth-century bishop and poet whose collected verse and best-known ballad bore these titles.

clue.text: Like Sebastian's stately home

parts.note: Sebastian Flyte's family seat is Brideshead, which Charles Ryder goes back to in the title of Waugh's novel

explanation.surface: Describing an aristocrat's country house.
explanation.walkthrough: Evelyn Waugh's novel is Brideshead Revisited; Brideshead is the home of Sebastian Flyte's family.
explanation.definitionFit: Waugh's title says the house was visited again, which is what the narrator does in the novel.

clue.text: Guides for editorials

definitions.meaning: people who go in front and show the way
in British papers, the main opinion articles are known by this name

explanation.definitionFit: Those who show the way are heads of a group; in British journalism the main opinion pieces carry the same name.

clue.text: Driven an exceptional version of Trojan horse, perhaps?

indicators.note: an exceptional version is an unusual rendering, so the letters of the words before it are rearranged

parts.note: the printed words, read as the setter meant them with a single N

explanation.surface: A remarkable new take on the wooden horse of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exceptional version of' rearranges the fodder, which should be DRIVE AN: the clue as printed has an extra N. The Trojan horse carried Greek soldiers who invaded Troy.
explanation.definitionFit: The wooden horse smuggled an attacking force into Troy, and a computer Trojan is likewise an intruder.

clue.text: Rebecca (of Sunnybrook Farm)

parts.note: the heroine of Kate Douglas Wiggin's novel; the clue asks for her surname

explanation.surface: Naming the heroine of a children's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: In Kate Douglas Wiggin's 1903 novel the heroine's full name is Rebecca Rowena Randall.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of the girl who goes to live with her aunts in Wiggin's American children's classic.

clue.text: Symphonic poet with Bohemian lifestyle

parts.note: reads as a free-living artist, but means a composer of symphonic poems who was literally from Bohemia

explanation.surface: An unconventional artist who writes in a grand style.
explanation.walkthrough: Bedřich Smetana, Czech composer from Bohemia, wrote the cycle of symphonic poems Má vlast; 'Bohemian' is taken literally, not as 'unconventional'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Czech composer of Má vlast, a set of six orchestral tone poems about his Bohemian homeland.

clue.text: A pirate in London

definitions.meaning: Jack London's novel The ..., about the brutal captain Wolf Larsen

explanation.definitionFit: A buccaneer is a predator of the seas, and Jack London titled his novel about a ruthless captain the same way.

clue.text: Section of church starting a perfectly sensible ecumenicism

indicators.note: the starting letters of the four words that follow are taken in order

explanation.surface: An ecumenical move that begins in a sensible way.
explanation.definitionFit: The semicircular recess at the east end of a church, usually holding the altar.

clue.text: Coin a name for Russian heroine

definitions.meaning: an old Indian coin, a sixteenth of a rupee
Tolstoy's Karenina, the tragic heroine of his novel

explanation.definitionFit: A former Indian currency unit worth a sixteenth of a rupee shares its spelling with Tolstoy's doomed heroine's first name.

clue.text: Bird shows a great deal of remorse

indicators.note: most of the word, with only one letter dropped from the front

parts.note: remorse is regret

explanation.surface: A bird displays deep sorrow.
explanation.definitionFit: A white heron with long plumes is a wading bird.

clue.text: More life was his, though its inspiration lost his head

definitions.text: More life was his, though its inspiration lost his head

parts.words: More life was his, though its inspiration lost his head
parts.note: reads as someone enjoying extra years, but means the son-in-law who wrote the Life of Sir Thomas More, beheaded in 1535

explanation.surface: A survivor who outlived the person who inspired him, beheaded.
explanation.walkthrough: William Roper, married to More's daughter Margaret, wrote The Life of Sir Thomas More; More, its subject, was executed by beheading.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname of Thomas More's son-in-law and first biographer, who wrote his Life.

clue.text: Sounds like he is objective in song

indicators.note: says the word worked out from the next words is heard in speech, not seen in print

parts.note: in the objective case, the pronoun he becomes him

explanation.surface: A remark that a man is the object of a song.
explanation.definitionFit: A song of praise, usually to God, sung in church.

clue.text: Irritable Grahame protagonist?

definitions.meaning: the Water Rat in Kenneth Grahame's The Wind in the Willows, known by this nickname

explanation.definitionFit: British slang for bad-tempered is also the nickname of the Water Rat, a central figure in The Wind in the Willows.

clue.text: Questionable books

parts.note: reads as dubious volumes, but means the writings of doubtful authority excluded from the biblical canon

explanation.surface: Volumes of doubtful worth.
explanation.definitionFit: Writings of uncertain authorship kept outside the accepted canon of scripture.

clue.text: Hardy hero had the last word in eponymy

definitions.text: Hardy hero had the last word in eponymy

parts.words: Hardy hero had the last word in eponymy
parts.note: the Scot in The Mayor of Casterbridge ends the novel holding the title office that names the book

explanation.surface: A brave man won the final say in naming something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardy' is Thomas Hardy, not 'brave'. In The Mayor of Casterbridge the Scottish rival displaces Henchard and becomes mayor, so he is the last to bear the book's title.
explanation.definitionFit: The young Scot who supplants Henchard in Hardy's novel and ends up as its titular mayor.
